Head of Sales, India at Indeed.com

2d • 

For years, digital skill demand in India tracked closely with the technology sector. However, we're seeing that correlation breaking down.

Our latest Indeed Hiring Lab research with the Asian Development Bank, drawn from over six million job postings across six Asia-Pacific markets, puts India at the top of the region for digital intensity in hiring, alongside Singapore. 

More than half of all job postings now ask for intermediate or advanced digital skills, and the growth isn't coming from the roles you'd expect. Education, insurance, healthcare, construction, and retail have seen some of the sharpest increases in digital skill requirements over the past few years. Teachers, nurses, retail staff, and insurance professionals are being asked to work with digital tools as a standard part of the job nowadays. 

The market is pricing this clearly too with roles requiring advanced digital skills carrying roughly a 31% wage premium over otherwise identical roles that need none, with AI capability adding a further 3.6% to 6% on top of that. 

What this tells us is that India's digital transformation has moved well past its established technology talent base. You can deep dive into the full report here:
https://lnkd.in/drtYnmKM

We continue to look into data centre jobs. The second instalment of our research series focuses on jobseeker interest. One key finding is that data centre jobs in the US pay a premium over similar jobs not at data centres. This is probably one reason why searches for data centre jobs have risen 8x since 2022. Data centre jobs also tend to offer better benefits than similar jobs.

So what's the catch? Data centre employers expect workers to be available for irregular work hours or on-call rotations more often than in other roles within the same occupation. For instance, IT professionals supporting a data centre are 40x as likely to have to work nights, based on schedule descriptions in job postings. 

So these jobs entail trade-offs between pay and benefits on the one hand, and work-life balance on the other.

Ageing populations are driving demand for doctors, nurses and care workers around the world. One interesting finding in our new research is how important international talent has become to healthcare recruitment around the world, with healthcare workers moving not just from lower- to higher-income economies, but also between high-income countries.

Healthcare has high barriers to entry (formal qualifications, registration requirements). Despite this, across the OECD, 20% of doctors and 9% of nurses were trained outside of the country where they work.

Indeed’s data gives us a glimpse of where future healthcare workers may come from. Hiring Lab's Sneha Puri and Callam Pickering have put together an interactive dashboard showing international jobseeker interest in healthcare roles across 13 destination countries, including the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy and Spain.

For example, as you can see below, 12% of inbound clicks on nursing jobs in Britain come from India.

These clicks are not the same as actual migration, but they provide an early signal of where healthcare talent may be looking to move.

Check out the dashboard (and read Callam and Sneha’s blog post) here: https://lnkd.in/gRFrKwu4

One really interesting finding in our new research on football jobs is that hiring by professional football clubs is becoming much more data-focused.

Football clubs in the UK hire for a surprisingly broad range of roles, especially off the pitch. Overall, job postings at UK football clubs have tripled as a share of all postings since 2018. 

What's fascinating is that a growing share of that hiring is for Data & Analytics roles. These now make up 3.2% of football club postings, more than double their share in 2018.

Anyone who has read Moneyball by Michael Lewis will be familiar with the idea that in many sports, behind the players and coaches, there's a growing workforce of analysts, data scientists, commercial teams and other professionals helping clubs make better decisions. Football club hiring may be a niche part of the jobs market but the composition of hiring reflects many of the broader changes in the economy - especially the growing importance of data & analytics.

As thousands of young people across the UK 🇬🇧 receive their A-Level results tomorrow, many will be thinking about what comes next: university, an apprenticeship or entering the world of work.

The latter is becoming harder. Graduate job postings in the UK are down 7% from last year and are at their lowest level for this point in the year since 2020. Summer jobs (another important entry point for younger workers) are also at a four-year low.

This is happening in a relatively weak overall hiring environment: UK job postings are down 11% since the start of 2026 and now stand 32% below their pre-pandemic baseline.

Young jobseekers are clearly trying to adapt. Searches for AI roles on Indeed have risen 7x since GenAI became mainstream in 2022, with “training”, “entry level”, “apprenticeship” and “graduate” among the terms frequently paired with AI-related job searches. 

But getting that first foothold in a labour market remains a challenge in an environment where hiring is cyclically weak, while at the same time, the skills employers demand are changing.

More about this and other UK labour market trends in Jack Kennedy's Mid-Year UK Jobs & Hiring Trends Report, titled "A Labour Market Under Pressure - And in Transition": https://lnkd.in/gbaERbR8

🚀 Today we're launching something new at the Indeed Hiring Lab: the Labor Market Outlook Survey, a quarterly panel - built alongside Pulsenomics - of more than 100 economists from places like Harvard, Princeton, Stanford, MIT, Bank of America, Moody's, and S&P Global. It's a forward-looking complement to the real-time hiring data we publish every day: where the numbers are now, paired with where this group thinks they're headed.

The first read splits cleanly in two.

📉 From a macro point of view, the panel is remarkably settled — they expect a gentle slope, not a downturn. They see the Indeed Job Postings Index down just 1.4% through June 2027 and unemployment drifting to about 4.4%. This is a labor market that has cooled, not one that's still cooling.

🤖 On AI, there's no such consensus. Asked whether AI will be a net positive or negative for employment over the next year, 52% expect at least a mild drag, 35% expect a net gain, and 13% see no effect - a panel of experts landing all over the map. What they do agree on is where the pressure falls: 57% expect AI to weigh on the wages of college-educated workers, more than for workers without a degree. The credential long assumed to be safe from technology is the one this panel worries about most. 

💡 The through-line: the story here isn't how many people are working, but where the work is moving - which jobs are being rebuilt, and who can reach the ones that need doing.

This is just the first quarter. We'll track how these views evolve as the data comes in. Full results in the comments. ⬇️

AI is creating a two-speed jobs market in the UK.

UK employers are creating jobs for experienced staff with artificial intelligence skills and cutting back elsewhere, according to Indeed data. 

Firms posted about 10% fewer vacancies this month than in January 2025. 

However, software developers -- whose profession has been transformed by AI and suffered dramatic job losses since 2022, are back in demand with postings rising 14%. 

Much of the increase came from senior roles and those directly linked to AI. This means many of these jobs will be out of reach for many, especially young people, Jack Kennedy told me.

Occupations such as IT and engineering, where AI enhances the value of experience by taking over routine tasks, are among the few that have held up since last summer. 

Elsewhere, from retail and manufacturing to white-collar roles that are more vulnerable to substitution like accounting or marketing, vacancies have fallen by double digits as employers take action to cope with higher employment costs and a more volatile economy.

Vom Indeed Hiring Lab ins Dashboard des Statistischen Bundesamts.

Immer wieder nutzt das ZDF unsere Arbeitsmarktdaten neben denen des Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis) zur Analyse der deutschen Wirtschaft. Als das anfing, habe ich mich sehr gefreut.

Jetzt nutzt das Bundesamt sie selbst.

Auf dem Dashboard Konjunktur des Statistischen Bundesamts steht seit Kurzem unser Indeed-Index zu den Stellenausschreibungen in Deutschland. Zwischen Bruttoinlandsprodukt, Auftragseingängen und Arbeitslosenquote.

Die Auswahl dort trifft kein Marketing-Team, sondern die amtliche Statistik.
Warum das zusammenpasst: Amtliche Zahlen sind präzise, brauchen aber ihre Zeit. Unsere Daten sind tagesaktuell. Nebeneinandergelegt sieht man früher, wohin sich der Arbeitsmarkt bewegt.

Dass es so weit gekommen ist, ist vor allem der Verdienst unseres Hiring Labs. Danke an Virginia Sondergeld, Dr. Annina Hering und Lisa Feist und an alle, die seit Jahren an diesen Zahlen sitzen, meistens ohne Applaus.

Wir veröffentlichen diese Daten auch dann, wenn sie unbequem sind. Umso mehr freut mich, wo sie inzwischen stehen.
